title: The Pael

explanation.summary: The Pael is the stem with a doubled middle consonant. Its forms differ from the Peal's in their vowels as well as in the doubling, and in the participle and the infinitive it carries clear marks of its own. This lesson teaches the Pael's four main forms and the way it relates to the Peal.

sections.heading: The mark of the Pael: doubling
body: In the Pael the middle consonant of the root is doubled, and the doubling is shown by a dot in the letter. The first consonant takes the vowel a. Compare the Peal perfect קְטַל with the Pael perfect קַטִּל: the root is the same, the doubled middle letter and the changed vowels are the signs of the stem. The same mark is in the Pael perfect of the verb 'speak', מַלִּל, and in the Pael perfect of the verb 'receive', קַבֵּל.

Not every consonant can be doubled. When the middle consonant is a ר or a guttural, it is not doubled and the vowel before it is lengthened instead. This is why the Pael perfect of the verb 'bless' is בָּרִךְ, with a long vowel under the ב, and the participle is מְבָרַךְ. The long vowel is in the place of the doubling and has the same function.

sections.heading: The four main forms
body: The perfect has the first vowel a, then the doubled consonant, then a vowel (i or e) in the last syllable: קַטִּל, קַבֵּל. Endings are those of the Peal perfect: -וּ in the third person plural (וְשַׁבַּחוּ 'and they praised'), -ְתָּ in the second masculine singular (שַׁבַּחְתָּ 'you praised') and -ֵת in the first singular (שַׁבְּחֵת 'I praised').

The imperfect takes the same prefixes as the Peal, י- ת- א- נ-, with a shewa, and the first root consonant takes a: יְמַלִּל 'he will speak', תְּקַבְּלוּן 'you will receive', יְשַׁנּוֹן 'they will change'. The first person singular is אֲחַוֵּא 'I will declare' and the first person plural נְחַוֵּא 'we will declare'.

The participle begins with the prefix מְ-, which the Peal participle lacks: מְמַלִּל 'speaking', מְשַׁבַּח 'praising', מְכַפְּתִין 'binding' (masculine plural). It is conjugated for gender, number and state like the Peal participle.

The infinitive is formed with -ָה or -ָא after the doubled consonant, and is found after ל-: לְקַטָּלָה 'to slay', לְכַפָּתָה 'to bind', לְבַקָּרָא 'to search'. The vowels of these forms differ from those of the Peal infinitive, and the ending is not -ֵא as in a Peal infinitive of a weak verb. There is no מ- prefix in the Pael infinitive.

sections.heading: What the Pael does
body: The Pael has no single meaning. In many verbs it makes a stronger or repeated action, in some it makes a verb that is a state into an action (a causative of the state), and in some it is simply the usual stem for a verb that has no Peal in the texts. The relation to the Peal has to be learned verb by verb.

Ezra 4:23 and 4:24 show the contrast in a pair of verbs. In 4:24 the Peal בְּטֵלַת means 'the work stopped', and in 4:23 the Pael וּבַטִּלוּ means that the officials 'made them stop'. This is a causative sense. The verb 'slay' has a Peal participle קָטֵל in Daniel 5:19 and a Pael infinitive לְקַטָּלָה in Daniel 2:14; both mean killing, and the texts show no regular difference of sense between the stems. Do not rely on a rule: look at what the verse says.
Several Pael verbs in the texts are verbs of speech and praise: מַלִּל 'he spoke', שַׁבַּחְתָּ 'you praised', בָּרִךְ 'he blessed'.

sections.heading: What the texts contain
body: There are 84 Pael forms in the texts. They belong to forty verbs, most of which occur only once or twice. Many Pael forms carry pronoun suffixes (יְבַהֲלֻנֵּהּ 'it will alarm him'), and the verb 'alarm' is the commonest Pael verb of all, with seven forms. Forms with suffixes are taught in A3.2; here the focus is on the plain forms.
The generated tables in this lesson are filled from these forms only, so most cells are dashes. That is not a defect: the Pael of Biblical Aramaic is simply a small sample of what the grammar knows.

misunderstandings: Do not take every doubled letter for a Pael. The Hithpaal also doubles its middle consonant, and it has the prefix הִתְ- to show it. A form without a prefix and with a doubled consonant is a Pael.
Do not expect doubling to be visible in every Pael. When the middle consonant is ר or a guttural, it is not written doubled, and the long vowel takes its place (בָּרִךְ).
The Pael is not always 'intensive'. For some verbs it is causative and for others it is a stem with no clear difference from the Peal. Give the meaning that fits the sentence.
A participle with the prefix מְ- is not always a Pael: the Haphel and the Aphel also use a prefix מ- in the participle. Look at the vowels as well.

deeper.heading: The Pael perfect and its two vowels
body: The last vowel of the Pael perfect is i in some verbs (קַטִּל, מַלִּל) and e in others (קַבֵּל). Grammarians treat the difference as one of the original pattern, and the Aramaic of the Bible contains both. For recognising the stem, the difference does not matter.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בָּרִךְ is a Pael perfect, third person masculine singular: 'he blessed'. The subject is Daniel. The middle consonant is ר, which is not doubled, so the vowel under the ב is long instead. The object comes after the verb: the God of heaven.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Then when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וּבַטִּלוּ is a Pael perfect, third person masculine plural. The root is the verb 'cease'. In the next verse the same root is used in the Peal (בְּטֵלַת, 'it ceased'). The Pael here is causative: the officials 'made them cease'. The ending -וּ is the plural ending, as in the Peal.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Daniel returned answer with counsel and discretion to Arioch the captain of the king's guard, who was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: לְקַטָּלָה is a Pael infinitive after ל-: 'to slay'. Compare the Peal infinitive, which would begin with מ-. The Pael infinitive has no מ-, a doubled middle consonant and the ending -ָה. The sentence says what Arioch had set out to do.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: And he shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the seasons and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.

examples.analysis: יְמַלִּל (3) and יְבַלֵּא (6) are both Pael imperfects, third person masculine singular, with the י- prefix and a doubled middle consonant. The first means 'he will speak' and the second 'he will wear out'. The sentence describes what the figure of the fourth beast does: both are future events seen in the vision.

examples.analysis: Look for Pael participles with the prefix מְ-. מְשַׁבַּח and וּמְהַדַּר are both masculine singular absolute. They agree with the speaker, who says 'I praise and exalt'. The participle here is a main verb in the first person; no pronoun is needed because the speaker is known.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots; and, behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.

options: the prefix מְ- and the doubled middle consonant
the long vowel after the first consonant
check.explain: The Pael participle has the prefix מְ- and a doubled middle consonant. The Peal participle has neither: it has a long vowel after the first consonant, as in אָמַר.

check.skill: A Pael that does not double.
check.prompt: Why is the middle consonant of בָּרִךְ in Daniel 2:19 not doubled?

quoted.title: Daniel

quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: because the verb is a Peal
because the middle consonant is ר, which is not doubled; the vowel is lengthened instead
because the verb is in the imperfect
check.explain: A ר (and a guttural) is not doubled, and the vowel before it is lengthened. The form is a Pael perfect all the same.

reading.why: The interpretation of the fourth beast has Pael imperfects for what the king will do (he will speak, he will wear out) beside Peal and Haphel forms, so the stem has to be named before each verb is read.
